questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Always keep in mind leaner bodies need more calories than __fattest__ ones.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4: fatter**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"fatter"** is the correct comparative form of "fat" and is appropriate here to compare leaner bodies with those that have more fat.

 
 
• **Example:** Always keep in mind leaner bodies need more calories than fatter ones.
 
 
 
• **"Fatter"** is the correct word here because it is a comparative adjective, comparing leaner bodies to those with more fat.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 4: fatter**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *Always keep in mind leaner bodies need more calories than fatter__ ones.*

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.

I have __never had__ and never will be dependent on him.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3: never been**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase "**never been**" is the correct form for indicating that something has not occurred in the past and will not happen in the future, which fits the context of the sentence.

 
 
• **Example:** I have never had and never will **been** dependent on him.
 
 
 
• **"Never been"** correctly connects the two parts of the sentence, indicating that dependence has never existed and will not exist in the future.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 3: never been**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *I have never had and never will been__ dependent on him.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "has never been"** (incorrect): This would be correct in a sentence that focuses on the present, but the structure of the sentence requires "never been" to show both past and future time frames.

 
 
• **Example:** *Incorrect: I have never had and has never been dependent on him.*
 
 
 
• **Option 2: "never has"** (incorrect): "Never has" would not be grammatically correct in this context, as it disrupts the sentence structure and verb tense consistency.
 
 
• **Example:** *Incorrect: Never has been dependent on him.*
 
 
 
• **Option 4: "was never being"** (incorrect): "Was never being" is grammatically incorrect because it combines past tense with a progressive form in an inappropriate way for this sentence.
 
 
• **Example:** *Incorrect: I was never being dependent on him.*

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

If I wrote an email / to my boss now, / he will react / by yelling at me tomorrow in the morning.

options.text: by yelling at me tomorrow in the morning.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4: If I wrote an email**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the phrase "**If I wrote an email**." The conditional sentence is in the past tense ("wrote"), but the result clause is in the future tense ("will react"), which creates a mismatch in verb tenses.

 
 
• **Correct form:** "If I **were** to write an email" (using the past subjunctive form "were" to indicate a hypothetical situation).
 
 
 
• **"If I were to write an email"** correctly uses the past subjunctive ("were") in a hypothetical situation, as we are discussing a potential event in the future, not something that already happened.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 4: If I wrote an email**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *If I were__ to write an email to my boss now, he will react by yelling at me tomorrow in the morning.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "to my boss now,"** (no error): This segment is correct as it clearly indicates the intended recipient of the email.
 
• **Option 2: "he will react"** (no error): This segment correctly uses the future tense, which is appropriate for the reaction to the hypothetical email.
 
• **Option 3: "by yelling at me tomorrow in the morning."** (no error): This segment is grammatically correct and properly indicates the manner of reaction (yelling) along with the time frame ("tomorrow in the morning").

questions.question:

• The correct preposition to use with "angry" when referring to a person is "**at**," which indicates the target of the anger.

 
 
• **Example:** Rahul was angry **at** his brother because he broke his pen.
 
 
 
• **"At"** is the proper preposition used to describe someone or something that causes anger. It is used in standard expressions like "angry at someone."

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 4: at**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *Rahul was angry at__ his brother as he broke his pen.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

• **Option 2: "of"** (incorrect): "Angry of" is not a standard expression in English.
 
 
• **Example:** *Incorrect: Rahul was angry **of** his brother.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: "on"** (incorrect): "Angry on" is not the correct usage for expressing anger towards someone.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom from the alternatives.

Rajiv will understand some day that all his friends are __fair weather friends__.

options.text: A friend who stays only when times are convenient
True friends help you when you need them
A friend who meets you only during pleasant weather

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Option 1** i.e. "A friend who stays only when times are convenient".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **"fair weather friends"** refers to people who are your friends only during good times and abandon you during tough times. (सुविधाजनक समय के दोस्त)

 
 
• **Example:** When Raj faced financial troubles, all his fair weather friends disappeared.
 
 
 
• **"Fair weather friends"** emphasizes the unreliability of such friendships, highlighting how they lack true loyalty. (अस्थायी दोस्त)
 
 
• **Example:** She thought they would support her in her struggles, but they turned out to be just fair weather friends.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 1**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Option 2: True friends help you when you need them** (सच्चे दोस्त आपकी जरूरत के समय मदद करते हैं): This option describes the nature of true friendship, which is reliable and loyal.

 
 
• **Example:** True friends stand by your side even in the darkest moments of your life.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: A friend who meets you only during pleasant weather** (वह दोस्त जो केवल सुखद मौसम में मिलता है): This option provides a literal interpretation, which is incorrect in the context of the idiom.
 
 
• **Example:** This explanation does not fit the idiom "fair weather friends".
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Friends generally have similar characteristics** (दोस्तों में आम तौर पर समान विशेषताएं होती हैं): This option is unrelated to the idiom and talks about the nature of friendships in general.
 
 
• **Example:** Friends with similar characteristics often share common interests.

questions.question: Select the sentence that has a grammatical error.

options.text: They have an information about the event.
The cat is sleeping on a mat.
She is an artist at a local gallery.
Can you bring me the keys to the car?

questions.solution:

__
 
• The error in Option 1 is the incorrect use of the article "an" with the uncountable noun "information." The word "information" is an uncountable noun and should not take the indefinite article "an." The correct sentence would be: "They have information about the event."

 
 
• **Correct sentence:** They have information about the event.
 
 
 
• **“Information”** is uncountable and cannot be used with "an" or "a." Instead, we use "some" or no article at all when referring to it in a general sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 1: They have an information about the event.**

 

**Complete Sentence:** *They have information__ about the event.*
